title: What Authority Does an Enforcement Company Need to Act?

body_markdown:
Before an enforcement company sends a copyright notice, negotiates a payment or licenses your music, it needs authority for that specific action. A monitoring contract alone does not necessarily provide it. Neither does access to your catalog metadata, a royalty collection mandate or a general instruction to “protect our rights.”


For labels, publishers and catalog investors, the central question is not whether a provider can find unauthorized uses. It is whether the provider can legitimately act on the relevant rights, through the proposed channel, without exceeding its mandate.


This guide focuses on U.S. copyright enforcement. Other jurisdictions and individual platform procedures may impose different requirements.


## Authority depends on the action, not the job title


A private copyright enforcement provider generally acts under a rights holder’s authorization, not government-granted enforcement powers. It cannot impose statutory damages, compel payment or seize assets merely by sending a demand.


Three separate questions determine what it can do: **Does the client control the relevant right? Has the client authorized the proposed action? Does that action require a lawyer or a legally eligible claimant?**


An enforcement company may have permission to identify uses and submit platform notices while lacking permission to settle claims, grant licenses or bring litigation.

Treat these as separate permissions even if one provider handles several stages. A broad service description is less useful than a mandate that identifies decisions the provider may make and decisions reserved to the client.


## Establish control of the exact rights involved


### Verify the chain of title


Authorization cannot supply rights the client does not control. Before delegating action, confirm the ownership or exclusive-right position through signed agreements and applicable schedules.


Relevant documents may include artist recording agreements, copyright assignments, publishing agreements, acquisition documents and exclusive licenses. Administration agreements require particular care: authority to administer royalties may not include authority to pursue infringement, settle disputes or license every type of use.


The enforcement company should be able to connect each proposed claim to the agreement establishing its client’s rights. A catalog spreadsheet can help organize that analysis, but it is not a substitute for the underlying documents.


Under[17 U.S.C. § 204](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/204) , transfers of copyright ownership generally require a writing signed by the owner or the owner’s duly authorized agent, except for transfers by operation of law. Assignments and exclusive licenses therefore deserve more than a metadata check.


Identifiers help match recordings, compositions and interested parties, but they do not independently establish ownership. Understanding[which music identifiers matter for enforcement](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/isrc-vs-iswc-vs-ipi-which-ids-matter-for-enforcement) helps keep identification evidence separate from legal authority.


### Match the mandate to the right, territory and period


A recording and its underlying composition are separate copyrighted works. A label’s authority over a master does not automatically authorize it to act for the publisher, and a publishing mandate does not automatically cover the recording.


The same separation applies to territory, ownership period and contractual restrictions. A client might control a recording in one territory, administer a composition for a limited term or lack authority over particular commercial uses.


An enforcement company should receive a rights schedule identifying the works, rights controlled, territories, effective dates and any approval requirements. Where ownership shares or co-owner arrangements matter, document what the client can authorize without assuming it can bind every other interested party.


For example, an administrator authorized to collect certain publishing royalties may not be authorized to grant an advertising synchronization license. The precise agreement, rather than the administrator’s title, determines the answer.


## What an enforcement company needs for a DMCA notice


A provider does not have to own the copyright to submit a compliant notice as an authorized agent. The relevant permission is authority to act for the owner of the exclusive right allegedly infringed.


Under[17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512) , a DMCA notice includes a physical or electronic signature of an authorized person, identification of the copyrighted work and material to be removed, contact information and required statements. These include a good-faith belief that the use is unauthorized and a statement, under penalty of perjury, that the complaining party is authorized to act for the relevant rights owner.


An enforcement company should obtain documented authorization before making those representations. A signed agency mandate is usually more useful than an informal email because it can define the catalog, platforms, rights and duration covered.


The statute does not prescribe one universal power-of-attorney form for every notice. Platforms may nevertheless require additional verification, representative documentation or particular reporting procedures.


**Permission to submit notices is not permission to submit unsupported notices.** Review ownership, existing licenses, the alleged use and applicable exceptions such as fair use. Section 512(f) provides potential liability for knowing material misrepresentations in covered circumstances. A match to an audio file is evidence of a use, not a complete infringement analysis.


## Define authority for demands, settlements and licenses


### Outreach and demand letters


An authorization letter can permit a provider to contact advertisers, identify the represented rights holder, request licensing information and communicate approved commercial proposals.


It should also state whether the provider may assert infringement, demand compensation, set response deadlines or refer matters to counsel. These are materially different activities from asking which license covers a campaign.


An enforcement company’s contractual mandate does not override unauthorized-practice-of-law rules. Whether a nonlawyer may draft legal demands or negotiate another party’s disputed legal claims depends on the jurisdiction and the work involved. Calling the activity “business outreach” does not resolve that question.


Distinguish approved factual communications from legal opinions. Assessing litigation exposure, advising on remedies and representing a client in legal proceedings may require appropriately licensed counsel.


The provider should accurately identify its role. It should not imply that it is a law firm, government agency or copyright owner when it is acting only as a commercial agent.


### Settlements, releases and payment collection


Settlement authority should answer more than “may the provider negotiate?” It should establish who can accept an offer, sign an agreement and release claims.


Define monetary approval thresholds, covered uses, payment deadlines and whether a settlement includes a future license. Reserve decisions about litigation threats, broad releases and disputed ownership for the appropriate client decision-maker and counsel.


An enforcement company authorized to receive payments is not necessarily authorized to waive claims or forgive unpaid amounts. Conversely, permission to negotiate a settlement does not automatically authorize the provider to hold client funds.


Payment handling should therefore be addressed separately: who invoices, whose account receives funds, what deductions are allowed and how reconciliation works. If lawyers handle funds, applicable professional and trust-account rules also matter.


A payment covering one advertisement should not quietly become a release for an advertiser’s entire campaign history. Make the release scope explicit before anyone accepts the money.


### Licensing authority


Licensing requires control of the rights being granted and permission to grant them on the proposed terms. Specify the media, territory, duration, campaign, permitted edits and any approval conditions.


For music used in advertising, distinguish the authority to license the recording from authority to license the composition. Do not promise clearance of rights outside the mandate. Any remaining approvals should be identified clearly to the licensee.


A decision about[when to enforce and when to license](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/rights-reserved-when-to-enforce-vs-when-to-license) is separate from the question of who may sign the resulting agreement. The team may prefer a commercial resolution while still needing the rights holder’s approval for its terms.


Past-use settlement terms and future-use license terms also need separation. Resolving an earlier dispute does not, by itself, authorize continued use.


## Litigation requires standing, not just an agency agreement


A provider’s authority to contact users or submit notices does not automatically allow it to sue in its own name.


Under[17 U.S.C. § 501(b)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/501) , the legal or beneficial owner of an exclusive copyright right may bring an infringement action for that right, subject to the statute’s requirements. The claimant must have a qualifying interest in the right at issue. Authorization to enforce, without qualifying ownership, is not a substitute.


An enforcement company may coordinate evidence and work with counsel while the eligible rights holder remains the plaintiff. A bare assignment of the right to sue is generally insufficient to create copyright infringement standing; proposed rights transfers need legal review rather than a template designed only to facilitate claims.


For U.S. works, registration or refusal of registration is generally required before filing an infringement action, subject to statutory exceptions. Foreign works require separate analysis. Registration timing can also affect available remedies, so review the relevant[copyright registration and enforcement requirements](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/copyright-office-basics-for-music-registration-and-enforcement) before escalating.


Standing and representation are different requirements. Corporations generally must appear through licensed counsel in federal court. Hiring a lawyer does not cure defective ownership, just as owning the copyright does not authorize a nonlawyer provider to represent a corporation in court.


## Build an authorization package before action begins


The practical solution is a documented authority package, not an unrestricted instruction to “handle infringement.” It should let an internal reviewer explain why each action is permitted and identify where approval is still required.


For an enforcement company, the package should connect the engagement agreement to a current rights schedule and an approval matrix. Keep any platform-specific representative forms alongside those documents.


At minimum, address:


-


**Rights covered:** Identify works, controlled rights, territories, ownership periods and exclusions.


-


**Permitted actions:** Separate monitoring, notices, outreach, negotiation, settlement, licensing and litigation support.


-


**Approval limits:** Specify who approves financial terms, releases, legal escalation and disputed claims.


-


**Signing and payment authority:** Identify who may bind the client, invoice users and receive funds.


-


**Delegation:** State whether subcontractors or outside counsel may act and what authorization they require.


-


**Revocation and handover:** Define when authority ends and how pending matters, evidence and funds are transferred.


The approval matrix can be simple. For example, a provider may send approved information requests, but a named business-affairs contact must approve every settlement and a designated lawyer must authorize litigation escalation.


Recheck the package after a catalog acquisition, rights reversion, administration change or termination. Authority that was accurate at onboarding may no longer support a new notice months later.


## Frequently asked questions


**Does an enforcement company need a formal power of attorney?** Not for every activity. U.S. DMCA notices can be submitted by an authorized agent without a universally prescribed power-of-attorney form. A signed mandate documenting the relevant authorization is still prudent, and particular transactions, platforms or jurisdictions may require additional documentation.


**Does a provider need a government enforcement license?** There is no single U.S. credential that authorizes all private copyright enforcement activities. The requirements depend on the work performed. Legal practice, court representation and certain financial activities can trigger separate licensing or regulatory obligations.


**Can the provider sue if the contract says it may enforce copyright?** That wording alone does not establish standing. The proposed plaintiff must satisfy the applicable ownership and other legal requirements, and court representation must comply with procedural and professional rules.


**Is copyright registration required before sending a takedown?** U.S. copyright registration is not generally a prerequisite to a DMCA notice. It is a separate issue from the registration requirements applicable to filing certain infringement lawsuits. The sender still needs valid rights-based authority and a supportable notice.


## Review one mandate before the next claim


Before authorizing the next action, ask the enforcement company to identify the controlled right, the document authorizing that action and the person empowered to approve the outcome.


If those answers are unclear, pause the affected step and have counsel resolve the gap. The goal is not the broadest possible delegation. It is authority that matches the rights, the remedy and the person making the decision.
